prompt.context: Due to the recent bankruptcy of a major airline, the aviation authority from Brazil recently opened an auction for landing and takeoff slots in one of the country's biggest airports. A slot is the right to land and depart from an airport during a given period of time. Green Airlines, a small, regional airline operating in the North part of the country, was offered 10 slots, for the total price of $100M. If Green accepts to buy the slots, it would have to operate them for at least 5 years. The owner and CEO of Green Airlines approached your firm looking for advice on whether they should buy the slots or not.
prompt.question: Should Green Airlines buy the 10 airport slots for $100M?

clarifying_info.a: An airport slot is a permission granted by the owner of an airport designated, which allows the grantee to schedule a landing or departure at that airport during a specific time period.

clarifying_info.q: Does Green Airlines currently operate in that airport?
clarifying_info.a: No, Green Airlines currently does not operate in that particular airport.

clarifying_info.q: Does Green Airlines plan to offer international flights?
clarifying_info.a: No, Green Airlines currently only does regional flights and has no plans to include international flights.

clarifying_info.q: Does Green Airlines have planes to operate the slots?
clarifying_info.a: No, Green Airlines does not have the necessary planes to operate the slots. Management will need to lease 5 airplanes to operate the 10 slots.
The $100M is a one-off payment due before operations start.

clarifying_info.q: What is the CEO's main objective?
clarifying_info.a: The main objective of the owner/CEO is financial gain.

clarifying_info.q: Can Green Airlines sell the slots?
clarifying_info.a: Green Airlines can sell the slots, but only after five years of operation.

clarifying_info.q: What happens if Green Airlines does not buy the slots?
clarifying_info.a: If Green Airlines does not buy the slots, they will be sold to another airline.

exhibits.title: Airline Competitive Landscape
exhibits.shows: A map of Brazil showing the airport selling slots and the main hubs of Airline A, B, C, and Green Airline, plus a table comparing key operating metrics across the four airlines.

framework: Market: Demand trends at the target airport, traveler profile (business vs. leisure), financial health of other airlines, whether bankruptcy is industry-wide or one-off
Competition: Number of airlines at the airport, slot concentration, presence of Low Cost Carriers, competitive pricing
Revenues & Costs: Passengers per slot (plane size × load factor × flights/day), ticket price, fixed costs (leasing, salaries, maintenance), variable costs (fuel, other)
Internal Capabilities: Operational readiness (planes, overhead, sales system, suppliers), strategic fit vs. current regional model, financial capacity to fund the purchase
Risks & Alternatives: Cultural/operational challenges entering a new region, alternative uses for the slots (sell to larger airline), other growth opportunities

questions.prompt: Estimate the monthly revenue from operating 10 slots.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the key revenue drivers: number of planes, flights per plane per month, seats per plane, load factor, and average ticket price. Strong candidates will note that Green Airlines would likely need bigger planes and lower prices to compete in São Paulo, in line with Exhibit 1 benchmarks.

math.setup: Revenue per month = # planes × flights/plane/month × seats/plane × load factor × ticket price

questions.prompt: Estimate the monthly costs of operating 10 slots and determine the expected profit in Year 1 and subsequent years.
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm airline cost categories: fuel, crew/salaries, maintenance and leasing, insurance, airport fees, overhead, and setup costs. Strong candidate distinguishes fixed vs. variable costs and accounts for the one-time setup investment.

math.setup: Monthly costs = fuel + other variable costs + salaries + maintenance & leasing + insurance/fees/others. Year 1 also includes a $5M setup investment.

questions.prompt: The operational result is zero (break-even). What alternatives should Green Airlines consider to make the investment worthwhile?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose two main alternatives: (1) improve operational metrics to generate positive returns (larger planes, higher load factor, ancillary revenues, cost reductions); (2) buy slots, operate for the mandatory 5 years, and then sell them to a larger airline at a significant premium. The key insight is that the slots are strategically far more valuable to Airline A or C (São Paulo hubs) than to Green Airlines.

questions.prompt: Management has exhausted all operational improvements. Calculate the value of the 10 slots for a large airline (e.g., Airline A) that operates 300-seat planes.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that larger planes generate higher revenues at the same cost base, producing a positive monthly profit. The slot value for a big airline is much higher than for Green Airlines.

math.setup: Recalculate revenue using 300-seat planes (all other assumptions unchanged). Then value the perpetual profit stream using a perpetuity formula: Value = Annual Profit / Discount Rate.
math.answer: The 10 slots are worth approximately $240M to a large airline.

questions.prompt: What is your recommendation to the CEO of Green Airlines?
questions.guidance: Candidate should synthesize the analysis: Green Airlines cannot profitably operate the slots on its own (break-even at best), but the slots are worth ~$240M to large São Paulo carriers. Green Airlines can buy the slots for $100M, operate them at break-even for 5 years (total cash outflow: $100M + $5M setup = ~$105M), and then sell them for a price between $105M and $240M, capturing an estimated profit of ~$135M.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternatives could Green Airlines explore to improve the financial outcome of operating the 10 slots?

categories.name: Revenue Improvements
ideas: Increase ticket price on select routes
Add non-ticket revenues (baggage fees, seat upgrades, onboard sales)
Offer travel packages or shuttle services
Increase load factor through dynamic pricing

categories.name: Cost Reductions
ideas: Use bigger planes to spread fixed costs over more passengers
Negotiate better lease terms for aircraft
Change fuel supplier or hedge fuel prices

categories.name: Strategic Alternatives
ideas: Buy slots and immediately sell to Airline A or C (if not restricted)
Buy slots, operate 5 years at break-even, sell at a premium to large airlines
Partner with a large carrier to co-operate slots
Use slots as leverage in a potential M&A or partnership negotiation

recommendation: Green Airlines should buy the 10 slots for $100M
Operate them for the mandatory 5 years at approximately break-even (net operating result ~$0, with a one-time -$5M setup cost in Year 1)
After 5 years, sell the slots to a large São Paulo-based carrier (Airline A or C) for a price between $105M and $240M
The expected profit from the sale is approximately $135M ($240M value to buyer minus ~$105M total investment)
risks: Airline A or C may not be willing to pay full market value ($240M) at the time of sale
Regulatory changes could restrict or devalue the slots
Green Airlines may struggle operationally to manage a major São Paulo hub with only 6 planes currently
Financing the $100M upfront payment may strain Green Airlines' balance sheet
Market downturn could reduce slot demand and resale value
next_steps: Secure financing for the $100M slot purchase and $5M setup cost
Identify and pre-negotiate with potential slot buyers (Airline A, Airline C) to validate resale value
Source 5 aircraft leases on competitive terms
Stand up operations at the new airport with minimal overhead
Maintain break-even operations and monitor slot market value over the 5-year period
